title: Jeremiah 2:1–13
context: The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah, sending him to proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem what the LORD says. The LORD remembers the kindness of Israel’s youth, the people’s love as a bride, and how they went after him in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown. Israel was holiness to the LORD, the first fruits of his increase; those who devour him will be held guilty. Then the address widens to the house of Jacob and all the families of Israel. The LORD asks what unrighteousness the fathers found in him, that they went far after worthless vanity and became worthless. They did not ask after the LORD who brought them out of Egypt and led them through the wilderness. The LORD brought them into a plentiful land, and they defiled it. Priests did not ask, “Where is the LORD?”; those who handle the law did not know him; rulers transgressed; prophets prophesied by Baal. The LORD will yet contend, even with the children’s children. Nations have not changed their gods, which are no gods, but the LORD’s people have changed their glory for what does not profit. The heavens are called to be astonished. Two evils are named: the people have forsaken the LORD, the spring of living waters, and have cut out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that cannot hold water. A spring of living waters is a source of fresh, flowing water; cisterns are tanks people cut to store water, and broken ones leak, so they cannot hold what is put in them. The charge is that they have left the LORD himself and turned to substitutes that cannot keep or give what they need. The marriage language of youth and of a bride is to be read soberly, as a memory of early devotion, not as a cue for graphic description. Kittim and Kedar, named as far points of comparison, are often taken as western coastlands and as a desert people of the east; those identifications should be hedged.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s word came to me, saying,” Jeremiah again reports a word that came to him. The speaker of the narrative frame is the prophet; the oracle that follows is the LORD’s speech, which Jeremiah is told to proclaim.

Arminian readers take this as a fresh word for Jerusalem, received and to be spoken, not a private reflection Jeremiah decided to publish in the LORD’s name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the heading as the LORD’s initiative: the word comes to the prophet, and the speech that follows is God’s, not first of all Jeremiah’s counsel.

Shared ground: chapter 2 opens as the LORD’s word to Jeremiah. There is no party contrast over the heading itself.

verses.text: “Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, ‘The LORD says, “I remember for you the kindness of your youth, your love as a bride, how you went after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem,” and then, “I remember for you the kindness of your youth, your love as a bride, how you went after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.” The first movement is memory, not yet accusation: early kindness, love as a bride, and following in a barren land. The marriage image is to be kept sober. It names devoted following, not a scene to be described in physical detail.

Arminian readers hear a real remembrance of early faithfulness, a love the LORD remembers, which makes the later turning all the more grievous and all the more a matter of the people’s own leaving.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the memory as the LORD’s own: he remembers the kindness of their youth and their love as a bride in the wilderness. The later charges will stand against this remembered devotion.

Both traditions read a sober picture of early covenant love. The verse is not a fork, and it should not be handled as graphic marriage language.

verses.text: Israel was holiness to the LORD, the first fruits of his increase. All who devour him will be held guilty. Evil will come on them,” ’ says the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Israel was holiness to the LORD, the first fruits of his increase. All who devour him will be held guilty. Evil will come on them,” The people are described as set apart, like first fruits that belong to the LORD. Those who devour Israel will be held guilty, and evil will come on them. The protection named here belongs to that early standing; the chapter will soon ask what has become of it.

Arminian readers take the holiness and the first-fruits image as Israel’s real early status, a gift and a calling they later forsook, not a status that could not be left.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear Israel described as holiness to the LORD and as first fruits of his increase, with guilt promised to those who devour the people. The lines record what Israel was, and what the LORD would do against the devourers.

Shared ground: Israel’s early standing is holy and protected. The verse does not yet name the later unfaithfulness, but it sets the measure for it.

verses.text: Hear the LORD’s word, O house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hear the LORD’s word, O house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel!” The call to hear is public and wide: Jacob’s house, and all the families of Israel, not only a court or a single tribe. What follows is a word they are meant to receive.

Arminian readers take the summons as a sincere call to hear, addressed to the whole people, who remain responsible for whether they will listen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a summons to the whole house. The word is the LORD’s, and it is issued to all the families of Israel, to be heard as such.

Shared ground: the audience is the people as a whole. There is no party contrast over the address.

verses.text: The LORD says, “What unrighteousness have your fathers found in me, that they have gone far from me, and have walked after worthless vanity, and have become worthless?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “What unrighteousness have your fathers found in me, that they have gone far from me, and have walked after worthless vanity, and have become worthless?” The question is sharp: no unrighteousness was found in the LORD to explain the leaving. They went after worthless vanity and became like what they chased.

Arminian readers hear a real charge against the fathers, a leaving that was not caused by any fault in God. The becoming worthless is the fruit of walking after vanity, a path they took.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same question as the LORD’s vindication of himself and indictment of the fathers. They found no unrighteousness in him, yet they went far and became worthless by chasing vanity.

Both traditions share the point. The verse is not a contrast over why they left; the LORD says they found no unrighteousness in him.

verses.text: They didn’t say, ‘Where is the LORD who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and of pits, through a land of drought and of the shadow of death, through a land that no one passed through, and where no man lived?’
verses.arminianNotes:
They didn’t say, “Where is the LORD who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness,” through deserts, pits, drought, the shadow of death, and a land where no one passed through. The forgotten question is the forgotten exodus and leading. They did not seek the LORD who had actually brought them through that land.

Arminian readers take the failure to ask as a real neglect, a refusal to remember the LORD’s leading, not an inevitable forgetting they could not have resisted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a failure to seek the LORD who brought them up from Egypt and led them through the wilderness. The long description of that land underlines what they had been given and did not remember.

Shared ground: the exodus and the wilderness leading are the LORD’s, and the people did not ask after him. The geography is the verse’s own, not a cue for a forced map.

verses.text: I brought you into a plentiful land to eat its fruit and its goodness; but when you entered, you defiled my land, and made my heritage an abomination.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I brought you into a plentiful land to eat its fruit and its goodness; but when you entered, you defiled my land, and made my heritage an abomination.” The gift is a plentiful land; the response is defilement of the LORD’s land and heritage. The land is called his, and what they made of it is called an abomination.

Arminian readers hear a real misuse of a real gift. They entered and defiled what they had been brought to eat, a guilty act, not a fate the land itself forced on them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the bringing in as the LORD’s act and the defilement as the people’s. The heritage is his, and they made it an abomination after they entered.

Both traditions share the charge. The contrast in the verse is between the plentiful gift and the defilement, not between the two later readings of grace.

verses.text: The priests didn’t say, ‘Where is the LORD?’ and those who handle the law didn’t know me. The rulers also transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal and followed things that do not profit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The priests didn’t say, ‘Where is the LORD?’ and those who handle the law didn’t know me. The rulers also transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal and followed things that do not profit.” The failure is named across offices: priests, handlers of the law, rulers, and prophets. Even those who should have known the LORD and handled his law did not; the prophets spoke by Baal.

Arminian readers take each office as responsible. Priests could have asked, handlers of the law could have known, rulers could have refused to transgress, and prophets could have refused to speak by Baal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear a comprehensive indictment of the people’s leaders. The LORD is not known where he should have been known, and the prophets’ speech by Baal is named as a following of things that do not profit.

Shared ground: every named group is at fault. There is no party contrast over which office failed.

verses.text: “Therefore I will yet contend with you,” says the LORD, “and I will contend with your children’s children.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore I will yet contend with you,” says the LORD, “and I will contend with your children’s children.” The contention is not finished. It will reach the present hearers and their descendants. The “therefore” looks back to the forsaking just described.

Arminian readers hear a real legal contention, a case the LORD still presses with this generation and the next, a warning meant to be heard, not a closed fate already spent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “I will yet contend” as the LORD’s settled purpose to press his case, even to the children’s children, on the ground of the guilt already named.

Shared ground: the LORD is not done contending. The verse looks forward in the book, and it does not require a fork over the word “contend”

verses.text: For pass over to the islands of Kittim, and see. Send to Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there has been such a thing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For pass over to the islands of Kittim, and see. Send to Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there has been such a thing.” The hearers are told to look far west and far east, and to consider whether such a change as Israel’s has been known. Kittim is often taken of western coastlands, sometimes Cyprus; Kedar, of a desert people toward the east. Those identifications are common and should be hedged; the point of the verse is the comparison, not a lesson in geography.

Arminian readers take the command to go and see as a real appeal to what can be observed among the nations, a measure against which Israel’s turning will look unique and culpable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a summons to consider the nations. The LORD’s people are about to be compared, to their shame, with peoples who have not made such a change.

Shared ground: the look toward Kittim and Kedar is a test. Exact sites may be left modestly stated.

verses.text: Has a nation changed its gods, which really are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which doesn’t profit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Has a nation changed its gods, which really are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which doesn’t profit.” Even nations whose gods are no gods do not trade them away; the LORD’s people have changed their glory for what does not profit. The “glory” is their God, set against worthless substitutes.

Arminian readers hear a real and astonishing exchange, a change the people made, leaving their glory for what cannot profit, not a swap they could not have refused.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the contrast as the LORD’s own amazement and charge: nations do not change even false gods, but his people have changed their glory for what does not profit.

Both traditions share the indictment. The verse is not a debate about whether the other nations’ gods are real; the text already says they are no gods.

verses.text: “Be astonished, you heavens, at this and be horribly afraid. Be very desolate,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Be astonished, you heavens, at this and be horribly afraid. Be very desolate,” says the LORD. The heavens are called as witnesses to be shocked and laid waste at what has happened. The astonishment is at the exchange just named.

Arminian readers take the address to the heavens as a way of underlining how wrong the people’s change is, a public shame, not a mere figure that softens the charge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a summons to the heavens. The LORD himself calls for astonishment and fear at what his people have done, and the desolation named is the fitting response to that act.

Shared ground: the deed is so wrong that heaven is told to be astonished. There is no party contrast over the apostrophe itself.

verses.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.” The two evils belong together. A spring of living waters is a source of fresh, flowing water; the LORD identifies himself as that spring. Cisterns are tanks people cut in the rock to store water; broken ones leak, and so they cannot hold what is put in them. The people have left the LORD and have made substitutes that cannot keep or give life.

Arminian readers take both evils as the people’s own doing: a real forsaking of the living spring, and a real labor to cut out cisterns that cannot hold water. The substitutes, whether idols or other trusts, are chosen, and they fail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear two evils the LORD names as his people’s: they have forsaken him, and they have cut out broken cisterns. The LORD is the spring of living waters; what they have made cannot hold water. The verse is a plain charge, not a puzzle.

Shared ground: the LORD is the living spring, and the cisterns are failed substitutes. The image should be explained in these plain terms, without turning it into a party contrast.
